title: Austerity of body, speech and mind

verses.sa: देवद्विजगुरुप्राज्ञपूजनं शौचमार्जवम् । ब्रह्मचर्यमहिंसा च शारीरं तप उच्यते ॥
verses.tr: Worship of the radiant beings, the wise, the teacher, and the enlightened; purity, simplicity, celibacy, and non-violence, these are called bodily austerity.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Listen closely for the word shaucham, purity, as Krishna lists what counts as bodily tapas.

body.text: Worship of the radiant beings, the wise, the teacher, and the enlightened; purity, simplicity, celibacy, and non-violence, these are called bodily austerity. The word shaucham, purity, is named here as bodily tapas. It shows that physical discipline is keeping the body clean and simple. Krishna now turns from the body to the tongue, defining austerity of speech.

verses.sa: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥
verses.tr: Speech that does not agitate, is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, together with study and practice, is called austerity of speech.
verses.angle: tapas of speech: calm, true, kind, and backed by study
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how inner discipline takes shape in daily life. He has just finished bodily austerity and now moves to how we use our voice.

body.text: Speech that does not agitate, is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, together with study and practice, is called austerity of speech. Krishna names the austerity of speech. It is about words that do not agitate the listener, that are true, pleasant, and beneficial. After speech, Krishna turns to the austerity of the mind, where silence and self-control take over.

verses.tr: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-control, and purity of feeling are called mental austerity.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Last time Krishna defined austerity of speech. Now he turns to the mind. Listen to the five qualities that make up mental austerity.

body.text: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-control, and purity of feeling are called mental austerity. The first quality is manahprasadah, cheerfulness of mind. It means the mind is not agitated or fearful, but settled and clear even in hardship. Krishna now brings these three disciplines together into a single sattvic way of life.

verses.sa: श्रद्धया परया तप्तं तपस्तत्ित्रविधं नरैः । अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्युक्तैः सात्त्विकं परिचक्षते ॥
verses.tr: That threefold discipline of body, speech, and mind, performed with supreme trust and without craving results, is called sattvic.
verses.angle: Paraya: supreme trust makes the discipline sattvic
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Why is some tapas pure and some not? Listen to the two conditions that turn discipline into sattva.

body.text: That threefold discipline of body, speech, and mind, performed with supreme trust and without craving results, is called sattvic. The verse names one quality, paraya, supreme trust. It is supreme trust placed in the practice itself, and that alone makes the threefold discipline sattvic. Krishna now turns to the next kind of austerity, the one done for praise and honor.

verses.sa: सत्कारमानपूजार्थं तपो दम्भेन चैव यत् । क्रियते तदिह प्रोक्तं राजसं चलमध्रुवम् ॥
verses.tr: Austerity done for honor, praise, and worship, or with a show of display, is said to be rajasic here. It gives unstable, temporary results.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now turns to the third kind of discipline, the kind done to impress others. Listen for the motive behind the practice.

body.text: Austerity done for honor, praise, and worship, or with a show of display, is said to be rajasic here. It gives unstable, temporary results. The Sanskrit word dambhena means with pretence or show. When austerity is done for this reason, it is called rajasic, and its results are unstable and impermanent. Krishna then moves on to the tamasic kind of austerity, one that is done with foolish stubbornness.

verses.sa: मूढग्राहेणात्मनो यत्पीडया क्रियते तपः । परस्योत्सादनार्थं वा तत्तामसमुदाहृतम् ॥
verses.tr: Austerity done with foolish stubbornness, by torturing oneself or harming others, is called tamasic.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Listen for the word pida, pain. How does the way pain is used here reveal the nature of this austerity?

body.text: Austerity done with foolish stubbornness, by torturing oneself or harming others, is called tamasic. The word pida, meaning pain, appears in the phrase of torturing oneself, showing that this austerity harms the one performing it. Krishna then describes the third kind of austerity, which is done to harm others.

verses.sa: दातव्यमिति यद्दानं दीयतेऽनुपकारिणे । देशे काले च पात्रे च तद्दानं सात्त्विकं स्मृतम् ॥
verses.tr: A gift given with the feeling that giving is a duty, offered to a worthy person at the right place and time, is called sattvic.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: After Krishna dismisses giving that harms others or seeks reward, he points to the purest kind of charity, one given only because it is right.

body.text: A gift given with the feeling that giving is a duty, offered to a worthy person at the right place and time, is called sattvic. The word daatavyam, to be given, shows that the giver acts from duty. They give because giving is the right thing to do. They do not give because they expect thanks or a return. Krishna then turns to the opposite kind of giving, which is done for a return or a desired result.

verses.sa: यत्तु प्रत्युपकारार्थं फलमुद्दिश्य वा पुनः । दीयते च परिक्लिष्टं तद्दानं राजसं स्मृतम् ॥
verses.tr: But charity given in return, or for a desired result, and given grudgingly, is said to be rajasic.
verses.angle: Pariklishtam: a gift given with strain
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna continues his teaching on the nature of giving. Listen for the exact moment a gift becomes impure.

body.text: But charity given in return, or for a desired result, and given grudgingly, is said to be rajasic. Charity given for a return, for a hoped-for result, or grudgingly, is what Krishna calls rajasic. Krishna now moves to the lowest kind of giving, the tamasic gift given with contempt and without respect.

verses.tr: Charity given at the wrong place and time, to an unworthy recipient, without respect and with contempt, is called tamasic.
verses.angle: Tamasam: the four marks of the lowest charity
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just described a giving that is mixed with self-interest, and now he names the lowest form. Listen to the four ways a gift can fail.

body.text: Charity given at the wrong place and time, to an unworthy recipient, without respect and with contempt, is called tamasic. The word tamasam, tamasic, appears at the end, and it is attached to four conditions: the wrong place, the wrong time, the wrong person, and contempt. The next verse moves from the act of giving to the three syllables that name the supreme reality.

verses.sa: तत्सदिति निर्देशो ब्रह्मणस्त्रिविधः स्मृतः । ब्राह्मणास्तेन वेदाश्च यज्ञाश्च विहिताः पुरा ॥
verses.tr: Om, Tat, and Sat are the three names by which the supreme reality is known. By that, the Vedas, the priests, and the sacrifices were established in the beginning.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna shifts the teaching from charity to the source behind all sacred action. Listen for the ancient names he names.

body.text: Om, Tat, and Sat are the three names by which the supreme reality is known. By that, the Vedas, the priests, and the sacrifices were established in the beginning. The verse pairs Om, Tat, and Sat as the three names of Brahman, and then links them directly to the origin of the Vedas, the priests, and the sacrifices. Krishna now says that all sacred acts begin with the utterance of Om, for those who speak of Brahman.

verses.sa: तस्मादोमित्युदाहृत्य यज्ञदानतपःक्रियाः । प्रवर्तन्ते विधानोक्ताः सततं ब्रह्मवादिनाम् ॥
verses.tr: Therefore, the ritual acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity prescribed by scripture are always begun by uttering Om, for those who speak of Brahman.
verses.angle: Udahritya: the sound that comes first
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just named Om, Tat, and Sat. Now he tells you that those who speak of Brahman always begin their prescribed acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity by uttering Om.

body.text: Therefore, the ritual acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity prescribed by scripture are always begun by uttering Om, for those who speak of Brahman. Listen for the word udahritya, having uttered. It shows that the sacred sound comes first, before any physical act of giving or sacrifice begins. He then states that seekers of freedom perform these acts thinking they are for the Supreme Reality, without desire for a result.

verses.sa: तदित्यनभिसन्धाय फलं यज्ञतपःक्रियाः । दानक्रियाश्च विविधाः क्रियन्ते मोक्षकाङ्क्षि ॥
verses.tr: Thinking “all this is for the supreme reality,” seekers of freedom perform many kinds of sacrifice, austerity, and giving without wanting the result.
verses.angle: Tat, the supreme reality, guides the act
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna speaks to Arjuna about the inner state behind every act. Listen for the word that keeps a seeker from looking back for a reward.

body.text: Thinking “all this is for the supreme reality,” seekers of freedom perform many kinds of sacrifice, austerity, and giving without wanting the result. Notice the word Tat, meaning that supreme reality. The seeker of freedom performs sacrifice, austerity, and giving without aiming at any result, because the act itself is the offering. Krishna now moves from the inner state to the outer word, sat, which names existence and noble action.

verses.sa: सद्भावे साधुभावे च सदित्येतत्प्रयुज्यते । प्रशस्ते कर्मणि तथा सच्छब्दः पार्थ युज्यते ॥
verses.tr: O Partha, the word sat is used for existence itself, for noble being, and for praiseworthy action.
verses.angle: sat covers existence, goodness, and action
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now names the word that covers all three, and he says it in one breath.

body.text: O Partha, the word sat is used for existence itself, for noble being, and for praiseworthy action. Krishna explains sat: the word covers what exists, what is good, and any action worth praise. Krishna now moves from the word to the quality itself, calling steadfastness sat as well.

verses.sa: यज्ञे तपसि दाने च स्थितिः सदिति चोच्यते । कर्म चैव तदर्थीयं सदित्येवाभिधीयते ॥
verses.tr: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and giving is called sat. Action done for that purpose is also called sat.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: How can a single word, sat, cover both a state of being and a physical action? Listen for the link.

body.text: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and giving is called sat. Action done for that purpose is also called sat. The word sat here is not just the fruit of a ritual or a donation. It is the steadfastness, the inner state of being in sacrifice, austerity, and giving. Krishna now turns to the opposite, calling action without faith unreal.

verses.sa: अश्रद्धया हुतं दत्तं तपस्तप्तं कृतं च यत् । असदित्युच्यते पार्थ न च तत्प्रेत्य नो इह ॥
verses.tr: O Partha, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and any deed done without trust are called unreal. Its fruit exists neither here nor after death.
verses.angle: Asat: the unreal fruit of empty action
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just defined true action, and now he warns what happens when trust is missing. Listen for the word he uses for empty rituals.

body.text: O Partha, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and any deed done without trust are called unreal. Its fruit exists neither here nor after death. Krishna calls all of it asat, unreal. A sacrifice, a gift, or a penance done without faith is not just empty; it is called unreal, with no fruit here or after death. Arjuna then asks about the exact truth of renunciation and relinquishment.

prev.title: As a person's faith is, so is the person
